tip: 'Te quiero' is literally 'I want you' – yet it's the everyday 'I love you' for family and partners. 'Te amo' is heavier, saved for deep romance.
'Estamos a veinte de marzo' is literally 'we are at March 20th' – Spanish states today's date with 'estar a', with 'we' as the subject.
'Se me rompieron las gafas': the 'se' + 'me' pattern marks unplanned events – the glasses broke on me.
Spanish tells time by subtraction: 'las cinco menos cuarto' = five MINUS a quarter. Past half past, count down from the coming hour.
'Por internet' – 'por' indicates the means/medium through which something is done.
'Contar' means to count AND to tell. 'Nos contó una historia' = he told us a story. English hides the same link inside 'recount.'
'Lo encontré' = 'it I-found.' Object pronouns usually jump BEFORE the verb in Spanish – you say the 'what' before the action, the reverse of English.
'Piso' = apartment (Spain). In Latin America: 'departamento' or 'apartamento'.
There's no 'we' here – the '-amos' in 'cenamos' does that job alone. Adding 'nosotros' would add emphasis, like saying 'WE dine together, unlike some people'.
'Ser' for scheduled events: 'La reunión es a las 3.' Use 'ser' for when/where events happen.
'Llamarse' can be reciprocal: 'Nos llamamos' = we call each other. Also reflexive: 'Me llamo Ana' = I'm called Ana.
'Contestó' isn't 'contested'! 'Contestar' just means to answer – no argument implied. 'No contestó mi llamada' = he didn't answer my call.
No 'on' needed: 'el domingo' alone means ON Sunday. The article 'el' does the job English gives a preposition – 'nos visitó el domingo'.
'Fui al mercado por mi madre' is ambiguous on purpose: for her sake, in her place, or even to fetch her. 'Por' bundles motive – English 'for' can't tell you which; context does.
The 'se' makes it nobody's fault: 'se cayó', 'se rompió' – the cup fell and broke all by itself. Spanish loves this no-blame 'se': things just happen, no culprit named.
'Se jubiló' comes from 'júbilo' – jubilation. Spanish literally frames retiring as bursting into joy: my father 'joyed himself' out of work.
'Quedar' here means to arrange to MEET, not to stay. 'Quedar a las seis' = let's meet at six – the all-purpose verb for making plans with friends.
Literally 'it makes two months that I don't see her' – present-tense 'veo', no perfect needed, because the not-seeing is still true at this very moment.
'Hace tres meses que empecé' = 'it MAKES three months that I started.' Spanish turns 'ago' into the verb 'hacer' – 'hace' + time up front, 'que' hooks on the event.
You can't 'want someone TO do' in Spanish. When the subjects differ it's 'que' + subjunctive: 'quiso que fuéramos' = he wanted that we-went.
'Por el cual' = for which, more formal than 'por el que'.
'Para' + destination = heading toward.
'Precioso' rarely means precious – it's the everyday word for gorgeous. 'Un cuadro precioso' = a beautiful painting, no gemstones involved.
Spanish has no verb 'to borrow' – only 'prestar' (lend). Borrowing is 'pedir prestado', 'asking lent.' 'Me prestó su carro' = she lent me her car.
When someone says 'nos invitó a comer,' they're paying! 'Invitar' means invite AND treat – accept the invitation and your wallet stays shut.
'Por culpa de' = because of (blaming). 'Llegué' = I arrived.
No 'I hope' needed: Spanish launches wishes with bare 'que' + subjunctive. 'Que tengas un día maravilloso' = (may) you have – the 'espero' stays silent.
Both imperfect: 'era' + 'vivía'. Habitual past – describes how things used to be.
'Se pintó LAS uñas' – the nails, not 'her' nails. With body parts, the reflexive 'se' already says whose, so Spanish skips the possessive.
'Asistir' doesn't mean assist – it means ATTEND. 'Asistir a la reunión' = go to the meeting. To help someone is 'ayudar'.
